claims.text: Hardness in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by composition-induced lattice distortion.
Strength in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by composition-induced lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion produces heterogeneous local stress fields that impede dislocation motion.
Atomic size mismatch can be varied through alloy composition to create controlled differences in lattice distortion.
Grain size and secondary-phase content should be held constant while atomic size mismatch is varied.
X-ray diffraction microstrain can be used as a measure of the degree of lattice distortion.
The atomic size difference parameter can be used to assess atomic size misfit.
Greater lattice distortion raises local stress fields.
The resulting local stress fields increase barriers to plastic deformation by hindering dislocation motion.
Alloys with greater lattice distortion will exhibit higher hardness than a baseline alloy with minimal atomic size mismatch.
Alloys with greater lattice distortion will exhibit higher strength than a baseline alloy with minimal atomic size mismatch.
Hardness and strength will scale with the magnitude of lattice distortion.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase, homogenized high-entropy alloys tested at ambient temperature and moderate strain rates where microstructural evolution does not dominate.
Solid-solution strengthening and grain-boundary effects may also contribute to hardness and strength.
High-temperature or cyclic loading may obscure the influence of lattice distortion.
Failure of higher-distortion alloys to consistently exceed the baseline in hardness and strength, after excluding grain-size and phase-structure differences, would falsify the hypothesis.
